content.p: Safsaf was a small farming village of olive trees, fig trees and vineyards on a low hill beside the road from Safed to Tarshiha in the Upper Galilee. On 29 October 1948 it became the first village taken in Operation Hiram, the Israeli offensive that overran the Galilee in the last weeks of the 1948 war. According to one of its fighters, the defenders withdrew to Lebanon and left most of the villagers behind. What happened to those villagers is known from fragments: notes written down by Israeli politicians in 1948 that survive in two versions, a diary kept by a Jewish National Fund official, the recollections of villagers given to a Palestinian historian, and a document that the Defense Ministry reportedly had locked away.

Those fragments agree on the core of the accusation. Soldiers of the Seventh Brigade are said to have separated the men from the women, bound the men, shot them and buried them in a pit, and to have raped women. They disagree on the numbers. No trial over Safsaf is mentioned in any page consulted, and the reports of the inquiries opened at the time have for the most part stayed classified.
content.h2: A village on the road to Safed
content.p: According to Walid Khalidi's survey of the depopulated villages, All That Remains, whose Safsaf entry Zochrot reproduces, the village's name means "willow" in Arabic and its Roman-era name was Safsofa. It paid taxes in 1596 on wheat, barley, olives, fruit, goats and beehives, and had 138 inhabitants. Late nineteenth-century travellers counted about 100. By the British Mandate every resident was Muslim, there was a mosque with several shops around it, and an elementary school had been opened. In 1944/45, 2,586 dunums were sown with cereals and 769 were irrigated or planted as orchards.

The same entry, citing the Palestinian historian Arif al-Arif, says that early in the war the village served as headquarters of the Second Yarmuk Battalion, led by Adib al-Shishakli, who later became president of Syria. The Arab Liberation Army was the force of volunteers from other Arab countries that had come to fight alongside Palestinians.

In October 1948 the Israeli army launched two large operations: Operation Yoav in the south, and Operation Hiram in the north. A Haaretz and Akevot Institute investigation describes the northern campaign as one in which dozens of Arab villages were overrun within 30 hours and tens of thousands of residents fled or were expelled. Within less than three days the army held the Galilee and had pushed into villages of southern Lebanon. Ilan Pappe, writing about an archive document, calls the operation "90 hours". The investigation says the overwhelming majority of the villagers took no part in the fighting and that most of the exchanges of fire were with the Arab volunteer force.

When the campaign began, about 120,000 Arabs were still in the Galilee, half the number who had lived there before the United Nations partition vote of November 1947. The advance put Israeli soldiers in direct contact with civilians, among them elderly people, women and children. At the war's end about 30,000 Arabs remained in the north, the Haaretz report says.

The village fell, in Zochrot's wording, some time before dawn on 29 October. Two platoons of armoured cars and a tank company from the Seventh Brigade attacked it. The Israeli army's own official history, according to the same entry, says only that the village "was occupied after a brief battle."

Villagers and a fighter later gave a different picture. One fighter quoted in the entry said the defenders expected to hold the village but were hit from three directions. He said that because no Arab army came to help, they pulled back with the volunteers to Lebanon, leaving most of the villagers behind, "many dead or injured".

The survivors' account, which the entry says was given to the Palestinian historian Nafez Nazzal, is that Israeli soldiers entered around sunrise and ordered the villagers to line up in the northern part of the village. A few soldiers then ordered four girls to carry water for them and instead took them to empty houses and raped them, according to the villager's testimony. The same witness said about seventy men were blindfolded and shot one after another in front of the village's people, and that the bodies were thrown on the concrete cover of the spring and covered with sand.

In the days that followed, Israeli troops came back and told those who remained to forget what had occurred and that they could stay in their homes. The villagers began leaving at night, about four at a time, until nobody was left.

The most direct written trace comes from a briefing given in November 1948 by Israel Galili, who had been head of the Haganah's national staff. Aharon Cohen, a member of the central committee of the left-wing Mapam party, took notes. As Haaretz quotes Benny Morris publishing them, they read: "Safsaf 52 men tied with a rope. Dropped into a pit and shot. 10 were killed. Women pleaded for mercy. [There were] 3 cases of rape. Caught and released. A girl of 14 was raped. Another 4 were killed." Zochrot quotes the same passage as a list of "crimes committed by the Israeli soldiers" and attributes it to Galili.

A second version, from the papers of Yossef Vashitz of Mapam's Arab department, runs close to Cohen's; Pappe says Vashitz quotes Cohen's notes of the meeting with Galili. Pappe, who posted it, translates it as: they caught 52 men, tied them one to another, dug a hole and shot them; ten were still alive; the women came and asked for mercy; they found the bodies of six old men, 61 bodies in all; three rapes, one of the victims a 14-year-old; four men shot dead; someone's finger was cut to remove his ring. Pappe describes it as an undated half page referring mainly to Operation Hiram. Both are a few lines of shorthand; Pappe describes the Vashitz page as undated. The wording is compressed and, as printed, the two do not agree on whether the "ten" were killed or were still alive, and the page does not explain the difference.

Yossef Nachmani, born in Ukraine, arrived in Palestine in 1908, helped organise the Zionist militias Hashomer and the Haganah, and from 1921 lived in Tiberias, where he bought land for the Jewish National Fund. In 1935 he began a diary that he kept until days before his death in 1965. After touring the villages taken in Operation Hiram he wrote of Safsaf. In the translation MERIP printed, he says the village raised a white flag, that the men and women were separated, that the hands of "some 50 to 60 peasants" were tied, and that they were shot and buried in a single hole, and that soldiers raped a number of the village's women. In the version quoted by Pappe, the count is 56 villagers.

Nachmani wrote of other places in the same passage. He recorded a "real massacre" at Saliha, with about 60 to 70 people killed. He asked where the soldiers found "such a degree of cruelty like that of the Nazis", and whether there was no more humane way to remove the Arab inhabitants. MERIP's reviewer notes that Benny Morris was the first to write about the diaries, in a Hebrew essay in 2000, and that the filmmaker Dalia Karpel brought them to a wider audience in a 2006 film.

Nachmani was not a hostile witness to his own side. The review describes him as a political moderate who spoke Arabic and had earlier proposed demolishing Tiberias's old city. The same reviewer sees in the Operation Hiram entries a man shocked by atrocities that his own life's work had helped make possible.

Safsaf was not the only village named. Haaretz and the Akevot Institute report that accounts of massacres reached the cabinet table in November 1948, and that the ministers' exchanges about whether to investigate were kept from the public for 73 years. At a meeting on 7 November, Haim-Moshe Shapira said such acts were forbidden "even in times of war", and the cabinet voted to appoint a committee of three ministers: Shapira, Mordechai Bentov and Pinhas Rosen. The report says they told the cabinet a week later that their powers were too weak to reach the truth. When the cabinet met again, Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion said that since the committee had not fulfilled its role, it was abolished. Interior Minister Yitzhak Gruenbaum answered, "We are burying the matter."

The cabinet then gave the prime minister the task of investigating complaints about the army's conduct towards Arabs in the Galilee and the south. On 19 November Ben-Gurion appointed the attorney general, Yaakov-Shimshon Shapira, who reported two weeks later. Ben-Gurion read the main points to ministers on 5 December, but that part of the minutes is still redacted. The Haaretz report says Morris petitioned the High Court in the 1980s for the report and was refused. The historian Yoav Gelber wrote that he had found no trace of such a report, and the Haaretz and Akevot report answers that it exists and that the minutes show the ministers disliked its conclusions.

The same report says that several ministers mentioned a code of silence among soldiers. Shapira told the cabinet that a soldier he asked to testify begged him to forget that he had spoken. It adds that the only combatant tried on murder charges over Operation Hiram was Shmuel Lahis, who commanded the unit behind the killings at Hula in Lebanon. No page consulted names a soldier charged in connection with Safsaf.
content.h2: The document that went into a vault
content.p: The Cohen notes had been published by Morris. Haaretz reported in 2019 that the historian Tamar Novick, four years earlier, had found a document in Vashitz's file in the Yad Yaari archive at Givat Haviva that described 52 men from Safsaf being killed. She asked Morris, who said he had seen similar notes, Cohen's. His book The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem cites Yad Yaari as the source of that other document, but when Novick went to look for it, it was no longer there. She was told it had been locked away at the Defense Ministry's instruction.

The Akevot Institute traced this to Malmab, the Defense Ministry's security department, which, the institute's report asserts, removed historical files from archives illegally and without authority and, in some cases, sealed documents the military censor had already cleared. Yehiel Horev, who headed Malmab until 2007, told Haaretz he had begun the project and that its aim was to undermine the credibility of studies of the refugee problem. The Haaretz and Akevot report of 2021 describes the Safsaf testimony as one "subsequently reclassified by the Malmab unit". Sha‘wan Jabarin, director of the Palestinian rights group Al-Haq, told WAFA that such concealment showed how serious the crimes were. That is his view.

The village never came back. Israel founded the settlement of ha-Shahar, later renamed Sifsofa, on its land in 1949, and a second settlement, Bar Yochay, in 1979. Khalidi's survey describes the site as overgrown with grass and scattered trees, with a few terraces and piles of stones from ruined houses; a few of the remaining houses are lived in by Israelis.

None of the pages consulted describes an excavation of the pit or gives a list of the dead by name. The contemporary notes give 52 men, with 61 bodies counted. The diarist wrote of 50 to 60, and the villager who spoke to Nazzal said about seventy. The gap is part of the record: what exists are notes of a briefing, a diary and a memory, and the reports of the inquiries that might bear on the count are, according to Haaretz, for the most part still classified.
